newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-WIFO stands by gloomy Austria growth outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-WIFO stands by gloomy Austria growth outlook.

text.p: Austria's leading research institute WIFO on Friday said it expected economic growth to accelerate next year but cautioned the recovery would be fragile, pointing to slack domestic consumption.
In its quarterly economic report, WIFO stuck to earlier forecasts that GDP growth would slow to 0.7 percent this year from 1.8 percent in 1995, then rebound to 1.0 percent in 1997.

"The economy bottomed out in the first quarter and we expect it to improve next year, but the upswing will be very modest because of the government's savings programme and pressure from weak domestic demand," WIFO deputy head Ewalt Walterskirchen told a news conference.

Buoyant exports would contribute to the upturn next year, WIFO's report said, noting that exporters were benefiting from relatively stable foreign currency markets and strong demand from central and eastern Europe. The institute saw exports rising four percent this year and 5.5 percent in 1997.

Domestic consumption, in contrast, had weakened after a promising first half. WIFO predicted that private consumption would increase one percent this year and just 0.3 percent in 1997, down from 1.9 percent in 1995.
"As a result, some branches of industry -- textiles, clothing, leather, construction, furniture and other consumer durables -- will see declining production," WIFO said.

The institute traced the drop to the effects of government savings and a higher tax burden from the beginning of 1997. Disposable income would fall 0.5 percent this year and 1.5 percent in 1997, the institute said.

The tourism sector, once the mainstay of Austria's economy but now in decline, was likely to remain in the doldrums in the short term, Walterskirchen said. The problem was structural and the industry would have to take sharper measures to become more competitive.
"Austria has rested on its laurels for too long as far as tourism is concerned. We must now look to other areas to compensate for the downturn in this sector."
The industry has seen revenues fall from 70 billion schillings ($6.54 billion) at their peak to around 20 billion schillings last year.
Inflation would remain at a modest 1.7 percent this year and next, compared with 2.2 percent in 1995, WIFO predicted.
"For a hard-currency country it (the inflation rate) is not as good as should be expected," the head of the Institute for Advanced Studies, Bernhard Felderer, said.

Overall sluggish economic growth meant there would be no turnaround in the employment market, with the number of jobless rising to 7.1 percent this year from 6.6 percent in 1995. In 1997 the figure would reach 7.5 percent, WIFO said.
Still, both WIFO and the IHS were cautiously optimistic about the longer term outlook.

"If we manage these growth forecasts there should be no problem meeting the Maastricht criteria," Felderer said in reference to Austria's efforts to meet the economic targets for joining a single European currency in 1999. ($1=10.71 Schilling)
